title: Devanagari Vowels & Consonants — Quick Chart
meta: One printable chart of every Devanagari vowel and consonant with its Romanised sound and an English word that holds the same sound. Free, no sign-up.
purpose: A single sheet to pin above your desk while the letter shapes stop looking like drawings and start looking like words. Pair it with the alphabet guide for the full explanation.

title: Reading Devanagari in a Week — A Practical Plan
meta: A day-by-day plan to start reading Hindi script in a week: what to learn each day, ten words to sound out, and the habits that make it stick. Free.
purpose: Reading the script is the single biggest unlock in Hindi — everything you look at stops being decoration. This is a one-week plan, not a promise: a week gets you sounding words out, not reading novels.

title: Hindi Sounds English Speakers Get Wrong
meta: The Hindi sound pairs English speakers confuse most — aspirated vs plain, retroflex vs dental — with minimal pairs to practise aloud. Free.
purpose: Hindi has a handful of sounds English does not. Get these six pairs right and your Hindi stops sounding like an accent and starts sounding like Hindi — this is the highest-value pronunciation work there is.

title: 100 Essential Hindi Words — Grouped to Memorise
meta: 100 high-frequency Hindi words in ten groups of ten — greetings, pronouns, numbers, time, family, food, places, objects, verbs, adjectives — with Romanisation. Free.
purpose: These are the words that do the most work in everyday Hindi — the hundred you should know cold before worrying about anything rarer. Grouped by meaning because memory likes categories.

title: Beginner Grammar Reference — One Page
meta: One printable page of the Hindi grammar you need first: SOV word order, noun gender, plurals, the verb 'to be', postpositions and adjective agreement. Free.
purpose: The whole skeleton of Hindi on a single page — the rules that explain almost everything you will say in your first months. Keep it printed; the deep explanations live in the guides this links to.

title: Hindi Postpositions — ka, ko, se, meṃ, par
meta: One printable table of the Hindi postpositions that replace English prepositions — ka/ke/kī, ko, se, meṃ, par, ke liye, ke sāth — with examples. Free.
purpose: English puts little words before nouns (in, on, for, with); Hindi puts them after. These postpositions hold most sentences together, and getting them right removes a whole class of early errors.

title: Sentence Patterns That Cover Most of What You Say
meta: Ten reusable Hindi sentence frames — 'I want…', 'where is…', 'how much is…', 'can I…' — that let a beginner produce real sentences from day one. Free.
purpose: Grammar is easier when it arrives as whole usable frames rather than rules. Learn these ten patterns and you can build hundreds of sentences by swapping one word — the fastest honest route to speaking.

title: 25 Essential Hindi Verbs — With Their Present Forms
meta: The 25 Hindi verbs that do most of the conversational work, each with its present-tense 'I' form (male and female) and a short example. Free.
purpose: A handful of verbs carries an enormous amount of everyday Hindi. Learn these 25 in the present tense and you can talk about your day, your plans, and what you are doing right now.

title: Polite vs Casual — Aap, Tum, Tu in Practice
meta: Hindi has three words for 'you', and picking wrong can be rude. A printable guide to who gets aap, tum or tu, with the verb forms that change with each. Free.
purpose: English has one 'you'; Hindi has three, and the choice signals respect or closeness. Using tu with a stranger is genuinely rude; using aap with your own child is stiff. This sheet gives you the safe default and the rules for each.

title: Restaurant, Shopping & Transport Phrases
meta: The Hindi phrases that handle a traveller's real situations: ordering food, asking prices and bargaining, finding your way, and taking a rickshaw. Free.
purpose: These are the phrases you will actually say on a trip — ordering without pointing, asking a price without confusion, and getting a rickshaw where you want it. Grouped by situation so you can rehearse each one.

title: First Reading Practice — Short Paragraphs
meta: Five short, graded Hindi paragraphs with Romanisation and English, plus questions and answers — your first real reading practice after the alphabet. Free.
purpose: The gap between sounding out single words and reading a paragraph is where learners stall. These five paragraphs are deliberately short and graded, so you cross that gap in one sitting.

title: Writing Practice — Form the Letters Yourself
meta: Guided Hindi writing practice: stroke order for the trickiest letters, copywork sentences, and self-check guidance. Print and write by hand — or type in the tutor. Free.
purpose: Writing is how the letter shapes move from your eyes to your hands — and handwriting fixes them in memory faster than reading alone. This gives you the order to learn the strokes, sentences to copy, and an honest way to check yourself.

title: The Mistakes Every Learner Makes — A Checklist
meta: A printable checklist of the ten Hindi mistakes that mark you out as a learner, with the fix for each — for revision before a trip or a lesson. Free.
purpose: Revision is most useful when it targets the specific errors you actually make. This checklist names the ten most common learner mistakes, why each happens, and the fix — tick the ones you have beaten and work the rest.

title: Family Words Quick Reference
meta: A printable table of Hindi family relations — mother, father, brother, sister, grandparents, and why Hindi has twelve words for cousin. Free.
purpose: Hindi family vocabulary encodes information English collapses — which side of the family, and older or younger. This table is the fastest way to learn the words you will actually need with relatives, and to see the logic behind them.

title: Work & Courtesy Phrases
meta: Polite Hindi for work: greetings, introductions, requests, agreeing, and the formal register — with the aap forms throughout. Free.
purpose: Work Hindi is a specific register: formal, polite, aap throughout. These phrases cover introductions, requests, small talk and courteous disagreement — the situations that come up in any professional setting.
